claim: The speakers say prompt optimization requires automated feedback such as tests or evals to direct candidate improvement.
Optimizing shared instructions or types for only one prompt can over-specialize them and reduce performance in other prompts that use them.
The described genetic Pareto search uses LLMs to propose prompt variants and retains candidates that are best on dimensions such as test success, token use, latency, or custom metrics.
The BAML demo gave the optimizer only source reachable from the selected function, including its inputs, outputs, and recursively referenced types.
The implementation exposed its candidate, merge, and reflection prompts as editable BAML and allowed different models to be assigned to optimization stages.
Greg reports that reflection improved after it received the full test source, because one failure message can omit later assertions and other intended behavior.
The live demo used existing BAML assertions as evals and named soft checks as weighted custom metrics without adding a new eval language feature.
The speakers recommend reading generated prompts because a small or unrepresentative eval set can reward accidental overfitting even when metrics look good.
The demonstrated optimizer required a user selection before replacing source and kept generated client type shapes fixed while allowing prompt metadata changes.
